title: Special Enrollment Period & Life Events Checklist
purpose: Students learn which life events trigger coverage windows, what happens if you miss those windows, and create a personal coverage timeline for their future.
learning_objectives: Identify which life events trigger Special Enrollment Periods (SEPs)
Determine the enrollment window length for qualifying life events
Apply SEP knowledge to real scenarios and understand consequences of missing deadlines
Create a personal coverage timeline with actionable steps
materials_needed: Two scenario walk-through worksheets (Sofia and Derek)
Portfolio deliverable template: My Coverage Timeline

key_concepts.special_enrollment_period: A time outside the annual open enrollment when you can sign up for health insurance due to a qualifying life event
key_concepts.qualifying_life_event: A major life change that triggers a Special Enrollment Period (losing coverage, turning 26, getting married, having a baby, moving states)
key_concepts.enrollment_window: The time period you have to enroll after a qualifying event (typically 60 days)
key_concepts.open_enrollment: The annual period (usually November-January) when anyone can enroll in marketplace coverage regardless of life events

life_events.notes: One of the most common SEPs for young adults. Coverage typically ends on your 26th birthday or end of birth month (check your parent's plan documents).
Allows you to add spouse to your plan, join spouse's plan, or get new coverage together.
Allows you to add the child to your plan or switch to family coverage.
Moving to a new ZIP code with different plan options qualifies. Moving within the same service area does not.

life_events.event: Losing a job and employer coverage
life_events.notes: Involuntary loss of coverage (layoff, hours reduced below eligibility) qualifies. Voluntary quitting may also qualify.
Income changes do NOT trigger SEPs. You can report income changes to adjust subsidies, but you can't change plans outside open enrollment.

life_events.event: Starting a new job that offers coverage
life_events.notes: Most employers have a waiting period (30-90 days) before coverage starts. Once eligible, you have a window to enroll.
If you choose to drop your plan mid-year, you cannot re-enroll until next open enrollment unless you have another qualifying event. Don't drop coverage without a replacement plan.

scenario_1_sofia.title: Sofia Turns 26
scenario_1_sofia.setup: Sofia turns 26 on April 15. She doesn't realize this is a qualifying event. She's uninsured from April 15 onward. On June 10 she breaks her wrist skateboarding and goes to the ER.

questions.question: When did Sofia's SEP window open?
When did her SEP window close?
On June 10, is Sofia still within her SEP window?
questions.answer: Yes—she has 4 days left (June 10 to June 14)

questions.question: If she enrolls by June 14, when does coverage start?
questions.answer: July 1 (coverage typically starts the first day of the following month after enrollment)

questions.question: What are Sofia's options on June 10?

options.explanation: She still has 4 days left in her SEP window. She should enroll NOW.
This would leave her uninsured for 5 months. Not advisable.
Depends on state and income. Worth checking, but not guaranteed.

options.option: Negotiate payment plan with hospital for uninsured bill
options.explanation: If she misses the June 14 deadline, this becomes necessary. The ER visit will cost $3,500-$8,000 uninsured.

questions.question: What would an uninsured ER visit with X-rays and a cast typically cost?
questions.note: Actual costs vary by facility and location. Some hospitals offer uninsured discounts or charity care programs.

scenario_1_sofia.key_teaching_moment: This scenario generates strong emotional reactions from students because they recognize it could happen to them. The 4-day window creates urgency. Emphasize: Sofia isn't careless—she just didn't know. That's why you're teaching this.

scenario_2_derek.title: Derek Loses His Job
scenario_2_derek.setup: Derek loses his job on March 1. His employer coverage ends March 31. He made $48,000/year before losing the job. He now has to find new coverage.

questions.question: Derek has 60 days from March 31 to enroll. What is his deadline?
Derek's former employer offers COBRA at $580/month. Why is COBRA so expensive?
questions.answer: COBRA requires Derek to pay the full premium (what he was paying + what his employer was paying). Employers typically cover 70-80% of the premium, so Derek's cost increases 3-4x.
questions.example: If Derek was paying $150/month and employer was paying $430/month, full premium = $580

questions.question: Derek checks healthcare.gov. His income for the rest of the year will be ~$0 (unemployed). Does he qualify for Medicaid?
questions.answer: Depends on state. In Medicaid expansion states, he likely qualifies (0% FPL is well under 138% threshold). In non-expansion states, adults without children often don't qualify for Medicaid regardless of income.
questions.action_required: Derek must check his specific state's rules on healthcare.gov or by calling 1-800-318-2596

questions.question: Which option should Derek choose?

options.scenario: If Derek needs continuous coverage for ongoing treatment with specific doctors
options.pros: Same plan, same network, no disruption to care
options.cons: Very expensive; not sustainable long-term without income

options.scenario: If Derek qualifies for subsidies based on projected annual income
options.cons: New network, may need to change doctors

options.scenario: If Derek's state expanded Medicaid and he qualifies
options.pros: No premium or very low premium, minimal cost-sharing
options.cons: Only available if eligible (check state rules)

options.option: Go uninsured until he finds a new job
options.cons: One ER visit or illness could cost $10,000-$50,000. Medical debt, credit damage, financial ruin.

questions.best_answer: Check Medicaid eligibility first. If eligible, enroll in Medicaid (no premium). If not eligible, compare marketplace Silver plans with subsidies vs. COBRA. In most cases, subsidized marketplace plan will be much cheaper than COBRA.

questions.question: What happens if Derek misses his 60-day window entirely?
questions.answer: He cannot enroll in coverage until next open enrollment (November-January, coverage starts January 1). He would be uninsured for 6-9 months, exposed to catastrophic medical costs.
questions.consequence: Medical emergencies, accidents, or illnesses during this gap could result in tens of thousands of dollars in medical debt.

scenario_2_derek.key_teaching_moment: COBRA is a safety net but almost always the most expensive option. Students should understand: check Medicaid first, then marketplace with subsidies, then COBRA as last resort. The 60-day window is critical—missing it has severe consequences.

portfolio_deliverable.title: My Coverage Timeline
portfolio_deliverable.instructions: List 3 life events from this station that are likely to apply to you in the next 10 years. For each event, write what you'll need to do when it happens. Be specific—include websites, phone numbers, deadlines, and action steps.

example.action_plan: 60 days before my birthday: check if my employer offers health coverage and when I'm eligible. If no employer coverage, visit healthcare.gov and compare Silver plans with subsidies. Check Medicaid eligibility for my state. Enroll before day 60 to avoid coverage gap.

assessment_criteria.accuracy: Life events correctly identified as triggering SEPs; window lengths accurate (2 points)
assessment_criteria.specificity: Action plans include specific steps (not vague 'get insurance'): websites, phone numbers, timelines (2 points)
assessment_criteria.relevance: Life events are realistic for student's age/situation in next 10 years (1 point)

final_reflection_question: What is one thing you learned today that you think most adults your age don't know about health insurance? Why does that gap exist?
sample_reflection_answers: Most people don't know that turning 26 triggers a 60-day SEP. The gap exists because nobody teaches this in school and people don't realize it's their responsibility to know.
I learned that missing your SEP window means you can't get coverage for months. The gap exists because the system is complicated and there's no automatic notification when your window is closing.
COBRA is way more expensive than I thought. People probably think they can just keep their employer plan after losing a job without realizing they'll pay 3-4x more.
teacher_notes: The Sofia scenario generates the strongest emotional reaction because the 4-day window creates urgency and students can picture themselves in that situation. Use it to drive home the importance of knowing your deadlines. Derek's scenario teaches that COBRA is expensive and marketplace/Medicaid are usually better options.
